claim: Daam2 is most highly expressed in low-grade glioma (LGG) and glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) across 34 malignancies in the TCGA pan-cancer expression data set.
source: we took advantage of the TCGA pan-cancer expression data set (Akbani et al., 2014; Weinstein et al., 2013) and evaluated Daam2 expression across a spectrum of 34 malignancies, finding that it's most highly expressed in low-grade glioma (LGG) and glioblastoma multiforme (GBM) (Figure 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 1A and cited references to the TCGA database.

claim: The majority of LGG and GBM tumors exhibited DAAM2 staining intensity scores that exceeded normal brain samples.
source: Notably, the majority of tumors exhibited staining intensity scores that exceeded normal brain samples, indicating that Daam2 expression is elevated within glioma tumors.
evidence: This is based on in situ hybridization analysis across 35 LGG and 40 GBM primary human samples shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: Daam2 expression is elevated in primary human glioma samples compared to non-tumor white matter.
source: In addition, we assessed DAAM2 expression via qRT-PCR in primary human glioma samples and non-tumor white matter, and consistent with the tissue microarray data, we found that Daam2 expression is elevated in a majority of these primary samples (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Daam2 exhibits elevated expression levels in mouse glioma tumors compared to normal brain tissue.
source: Combining this model, with our the Daam2-LacZ mouse line, we performed immunostaining on the resultant tumors, finding that Daam2 exhibits elevated expression levels in tumors, compared to normal brain tissue (Figure 1D; Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Daam2 is highly expressed in xenograft tumors generated from primary human GBM cell lines.
source: Finally, we evaluated Daam2 expression in xenograft tumors generated from primary human GBM cell lines, finding that Daam2 is also highly expressed in these human cell line models (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Daam2 accelerates the rate of cell growth in human GBM cell lines in vitro.
source: To assess its role in glioma, we performed overexpression, gain-of-function (GOF) studies in human GBM cell lines, finding that Daam2 accelerates the rate of cell growth in vitro (Figure 2A–B,F).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assays shown in Figure 2A-B,F.

claim: Daam2 accelerates anchorage independent colony formation in soft agar assays.
source: Next, we determined how Daam2 influences anchorage independent growth, via soft agar assay, finding that it also accelerates colony formation (Figure 2C–E).
evidence: Supported by soft agar assay data shown in Figure 2C-E.

claim: Combined overexpression of Daam2 in the PB-Ras model resulted in an acceleration of tumorigenesis.
source: Combining PiggyBac-mediated overexpression of Daam2 with this Ras-driven model resulted in an acceleration of tumorigenesis (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Combined overexpression of Daam2 in the CRISPR/IUE model resulted in accelerated tumorigenesis.
source: Consistent with the Ras model, combined overexpression of Daam2 in the CRISPR/IUE model, also resulted in accelerated tumorigenesis (Figure 2G–I).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 2G-I.

claim: Overexpression of Daam2 results in an increase in the number of BrdU-expressing cells in mouse glioma models.
source: BrdU labeling analysis of the resulting tumors from both models revealed that overexpression of Daam2 results in an increase in the number BrdU-expressing cells (Figure 2J–L; Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by BrdU immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 2J-L and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Decreased expression of Daam2 via shRNAi inhibited the rate of growth of human GBM cell lines in vitro.
source: In human GBM cell lines we performed shRNAi-mediated knockdown of human Daam2, finding that decreased expression of Daam2 inhibited their rate of growth in vitro (Figure 3A–B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR and cell proliferation data shown in Figure 3A-B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Knockdown of Daam2 resulted in a significant decrease in tumor growth in vivo in xenograft models.
source: Next, we assessed the tumorigenic potential of these GBM cell lines, finding that knockdown of Daam2 resulted in a significant decrease in tumor growth in vivo (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: Mice lacking Daam2 demonstrated decreased rates of tumor formation in the CRISPR/IUE model compared to heterozygote controls.
source: As shown in Figure 3F–H, mice lacking Daam2 demonstrated decreased rates of tumor formation in this model compared to the heterozygote control.
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging data shown in Figure 3F-H.

claim: BrdU labeling revealed substantial decreases in the number of proliferating cells in Daam2−/− tumors.
source: Moreover, BrdU labeling revealed substantial decreases in the number of proliferating cells in Daam2−/− tumors (Figure 3I–K).
evidence: Supported by BrdU immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3I-K.

claim: Modulation of Daam2 expression has a modest effect on Wnt activity in glioma cell lines.
source: To evaluate Wnt-activity we used an established Wnt-reporter (TOP-FLASH) and found that modulation of Daam2 expression has a modest effect on Wnt activity in glioma cell lines and did not impact Wnt activity in our mouse model of glioma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by TOP-FLASH reporter assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Modulation of Daam2 expression did not impact Wnt activity in the mouse model of glioma.
source: To evaluate Wnt-activity we used an established Wnt-reporter (TOP-FLASH) and found that modulation of Daam2 expression has a modest effect on Wnt activity in glioma cell lines and did not impact Wnt activity in our mouse model of glioma (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by FACS analysis of TOP-FLASH-BFP expressing cells shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: RPPA analysis revealed a cohort of proteins that are strongly downregulated in glioma samples that overexpress Daam2.
source: To identify changes in protein expression associated with Daam2-mediated tumorigenesis we performed reverse phase protein lysate microarray (RPPA) on FACS-isolated mouse glioma samples that overexpress Daam2. Analysis revealed a cohort of proteins that are strongly downregulated in glioma samples that overexpress Daam2 (Figure 4A; Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by RPPA data shown in Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1, and Supplementary file 1.

claim: VHL is one of the proteins with the most significant inverse correlation with Daam2 expression across a spectrum of human malignancies.
source: This analysis identified von Hippel Landau (VHL) as one of the proteins from this cohort with the most significant inverse correlation score across this spectrum of malignancies, with lung adenocarcinoma and GBM demonstrating the strongest negative correlations between Daam2 and VHL (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Daam2 expression was positively correlated with HIF1α and pAkt protein expression across a cohort of human malignancies.
source: Analysis of these data revealed that Daam2 expression was positively correlated with HIF1α and pAkt protein expression across this cohort of malignancies, with GBM and lung adenocarcinoma also showing the strongest positive correlation (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of TCGA data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: VHL expression was dramatically reduced in Daam2-GOF tumors.
source: Immunostaining for VHL in these models corroborated our RPPA data, where VHL expression was dramatically reduced in Daam2-GOF tumors, and increased in the Daam2−/− tumors (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: VHL expression was increased in Daam2−/− tumors.
source: Immunostaining for VHL in these models corroborated our RPPA data, where VHL expression was dramatically reduced in Daam2-GOF tumors, and increased in the Daam2−/− tumors (Figure 4C–F).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4C-F.

claim: Elevated levels of VHL protein were observed in the brains of Daam2-/- mice.
source: In addition, we also observed elevated levels of VHL protein in the brains of Daam2-/- mice, further reinforcing these expression dynamics (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: pAkt and HIF1α demonstrated elevated levels of expression in the Daam2-GOF tumors.
source: Next we assessed expression of VHL's downstream effectors, pAkt and HIF1α, finding that both of these proteins demonstrated elevated levels of expression in the Daam2-GOF tumors, and pAkt having decreased levels in the Daam2−/− tumors (Figure 4G–K).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry and immunoblot data shown in Figure 4G-K.

claim: pAkt had decreased levels in the Daam2−/− tumors.
source: Next we assessed expression of VHL's downstream effectors, pAkt and HIF1α, finding that both of these proteins demonstrated elevated levels of expression in the Daam2-GOF tumors, and pAkt having decreased levels in the Daam2−/− tumors (Figure 4G–K).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4G-K.

claim: HIF1α target genes Glut1 and VEGFA demonstrate increased expression in Daam2-GOF tumors.
source: Therefore we assessed the expression of HIF1α targets Glut1 and VEGFA in the Daam2-GOF tumors, finding that these proteins also demonstrate increased expression (Figure 4K).
evidence: Supported by immunoblot data shown in Figure 4K.

claim: Elevated levels of angiogenesis were detected in Daam2-GOF tumors via CD31 staining.
source: Finally, one consequence of these changes in gene expression is elevated levels of angiogenesis (Fan et al., 2014; Keith and Simon, 2007; Semenza, 2004), which we detected in Daam2-GOF tumors via staining for the endothelial marker, CD31 (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by CD31 immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3 and cited references.

claim: VHL suppresses the increased rate of cell growth mediated by Daam2-alone in human GBM cell lines.
source: To determine whether an epistatic relationship exists, we overexpressed VHL in the presence of Daam2 overexpression in human GBM cell lines, finding that VHL suppresses the increased rate of cell growth mediated by Daam2-alone (Figure 5A–C).
evidence: Supported by cell proliferation assay data shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Combined overexpression of VHL with Daam2 suppressed the accelerated rate of tumorigenesis mediated by Daam2-alone in mouse models of glioma.
source: Next, we extended these studies to our mouse models of glioma, finding that combined overexpression of VHL with Daam2 similarly suppressed the accelerated rate of tumorigenesis and proliferation mediated by Daam2-alone (Figure 5D–O; T-V).
evidence: Supported by bioluminescence imaging and BrdU data shown in Figure 5D-O, T-V.

claim: Overexpression of VHL resulted in concordant suppression of pAkt and angiogenesis in mouse glioma tumors.
source: Moreover, overexpression of VHL resulted in concordant suppression of pAkt and angiogenesis in these tumors (Figure 5P–S; Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 5P-S and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Daam2 co-immunoprecipitates with VHL in protein lysates extracted from the PB-Ras model of glioma.
source: Using protein lysates extracted from our PB-Ras model of glioma, we found that Daam2 co-immunoprecipitates with VHL (and vice versa), suggesting that these proteins associate (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: VHL degradation is enhanced in the presence of Daam2 in cyclohexamide-mediated degradation assays.
source: To test this we co-transfected Daam2 and VHL in 293 cells, and measured the rate of cyclohexamide-mediated degradation, finding that VHL degradation is enhanced in the presence of Daam2 (Figure 6B,D).
evidence: Supported by cycloheximide chase assay data shown in Figure 6B,D.

claim: The half-life of VHL (5.082 hr) was significantly decreased in the presence of Daam2 (3.679 hr).
source: Quantification in D shows the effect of Daam2 on VHL stability. Half-life of VHL (5.082 hr) was significantly decreased in the presence of Daam2 (3.679 hr).
evidence: Supported by quantification of cycloheximide chase assay shown in Figure 6D.

claim: In the presence of elevated levels of Daam2, the extent of VHL ubiquitination is substantially increased.
source: Using in vitro systems, we found that in the presence of elevated levels of Daam2, the extent of VHL ubiquitination is substantially increased and levels of VHL protein demonstrate a concomitantly decrease (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Levels of VHL protein demonstrate a concomitant decrease in the presence of elevated levels of Daam2.
source: Using in vitro systems, we found that in the presence of elevated levels of Daam2, the extent of VHL ubiquitination is substantially increased and levels of VHL protein demonstrate a concomitantly decrease (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination assay data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: VHL is a potent tumor suppressor regulating numerous pathways that drive cancer.
source: Von Hippel-Landau (VHL) protein is a potent tumor suppressor regulating numerous pathways that drive cancer, but mutations in VHL are restricted to limited subsets of malignancies.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about VHL function.

claim: Mutations in VHL are restricted to limited subsets of malignancies.
source: Von Hippel-Landau (VHL) protein is a potent tumor suppressor regulating numerous pathways that drive cancer, but mutations in VHL are restricted to limited subsets of malignancies.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about VHL mutations in cancer.

claim: Daam2 promotes glioma formation.
source: Using developmental processes to uncover new pathways contributing to tumorigenesis, we found that Daam2 promotes glioma formation.
evidence: This is supported by multiple functional studies in human and mouse models shown throughout the manuscript.

claim: There is an inverse correlation between Daam2 and VHL expression across a host of cancers, including glioma.
source: Protein expression screening identified an inverse correlation between Daam2 and VHL expression across a host of cancers, including glioma.
evidence: Supported by RPPA screening and TCGA data analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: Daam2 promotes tumorigenesis by suppressing VHL expression.
source: These in silico insights guided corroborating functional studies, which revealed that Daam2 promotes tumorigenesis by suppressing VHL expression.
evidence: Supported by functional studies in mouse models shown in Figures 4 and 5.

claim: Daam2 associates with VHL.
source: Furthermore, biochemical analyses demonstrate that Daam2 associates with VHL and facilitates its ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Daam2 facilitates VHL ubiquitination and degradation.
source: Furthermore, biochemical analyses demonstrate that Daam2 associates with VHL and facilitates its ubiquitination and degradation.
evidence: Supported by ubiquitination and degradation assays shown in Figure 6B-D.

claim: Tumor suppressor and oncogenic pathways function in part by subverting existing cellular programs to promote cancer 'hallmark' properties.
source: Tumor suppressor and oncogenic pathways function in part by subverting existing cellular programs to promote cancer 'hallmark' properties that engender malignant growth (Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge cited from Hanahan and Weinberg, 2011.

claim: Genetic mutation is not the sole source of dysregulation in tumorigenic pathways.
source: Importantly, genetic mutation is not the sole source of this dysregulation, as changes in gene expression via promoter methylation or protein turnover can phenotypically resemble driver mutations and contribute to tumorigenesis (Esteller et al., 1999; Hegi et al., 2004; Pineda et al., 2015; Reinstein and Ciechanover, 2006; Semenza, 2003; Shen et al., 2005; Zöchbauer-Müller et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: VHL is mutated in Von Hippel-Landau disease, a hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome that often manifests as clear-cell renal carcinoma (ccRCC).
source: VHL is a key tumor suppressor that is mutated in Von Hippel-Landau disease, a hereditary cancer predisposition syndrome that often manifests as clear-cell renal carcinoma (ccRCC) (Chen et al., 1995; Gossage et al., 2015; Kim and Kaelin, 2004; Maher et al., 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: VHL functions by binding to HIF1α and hydroxylated Akt and modulating their degradation and activity, respectively.
source: VHL functions by binding to HIF1α and hydroxylated Akt and modulating their degradation and activity, respectively.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHL function.

claim: Mutant forms of VHL associated with ccRCC are incapable of binding HIF1α or pAkt.
source: Mutant forms of VHL associated with ccRCC are incapable of binding HIF1α or pAkt, resulting in stabilized expression and activation of these proteins, which ultimately facilitates tumorigenesis (Guo et al., 2016; Ivan et al., 2001; Jaakkola et al., 2001; Maxwell et al., 1999; Min et al., 2002; Ohh et al., 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Dysregulated HIF1α and pAkt are associated with most forms of cancer.
source: While dysregulated HIF1α and pAkt are associated with most forms of cancer, mutations in VHL are found predominately in ccRCC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about cancer biology.

claim: Mutations in VHL are found predominately in ccRCC.
source: While dysregulated HIF1α and pAkt are associated with most forms of cancer, mutations in VHL are found predominately in ccRCC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHL mutations.

claim: ID2 can interfere with VHL activity in glioma cell lines.
source: Indeed recent studies in glioma have shown that ID2 can interfere with VHL activity in cell lines (Lee et al., 2016) and that it's subject to regulation by microRNAs (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2016 and Li et al., 2017.

claim: VHL is subject to regulation by microRNAs.
source: Indeed recent studies in glioma have shown that ID2 can interfere with VHL activity in cell lines (Lee et al., 2016) and that it's subject to regulation by microRNAs (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2017.

claim: Developmental processes directly contribute to all forms of malignancy.
source: Developmental processes directly contribute to all forms of malignancy and are utilized by tumorigenic pathways to maintain cells in an undifferentiated and proliferative state (Jackson et al., 2006; Kesari et al., 2005; Stiles and Rowitch, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Daam2 is a key developmental regulator that suppresses glial differentiation.
source: As a molecular entry point for these studies, we focused on Daam2, a key developmental regulator that suppresses glial differentiation and also contributes to dorsal patterning in the developing CNS (Lee et al., 2015; Lee and Deneen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015 and Lee and Deneen, 2012.

claim: Daam2 contributes to dorsal patterning in the developing CNS.
source: As a molecular entry point for these studies, we focused on Daam2, a key developmental regulator that suppresses glial differentiation and also contributes to dorsal patterning in the developing CNS (Lee et al., 2015; Lee and Deneen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2015 and Lee and Deneen, 2012.

claim: The CRISPR/IUE model closely resembles the genetics of GBM.
source: This model closely resembles the genetics of GBM (Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2005) and begins producing tumors detectable around post-natal week 8.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2005.

claim: The CRISPR/IUE model begins producing tumors detectable around post-natal week 8.
source: This model closely resembles the genetics of GBM (Alcantara Llaguno et al., 2009; Kwon et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2005) and begins producing tumors detectable around post-natal week 8.
evidence: This is based on observations from the model system described in the manuscript.

claim: The PB-Ras model generates malignant glioma in mice around post-natal day 14.
source: The first model combines targeted PiggyBac overexpression of oncogenic Ras-V12 (PB-Ras) in glial precursors with IUE, to generate malignant glioma in mice around post-natal day 14 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on observations from the model system shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Daam2 functions as a positive regulator of Wnt-signaling in the developing CNS.
source: Previously, we found that Daam2 functions as a positive regulator of Wnt-signaling in the developing CNS (Lee and Deneen, 2012), suggesting that it may also function in this manner in glioma.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee and Deneen, 2012.

claim: Daam2 potentiates canonical Wnt signaling through the clustering of existing Wnt receptor complexes.
source: Our previous studies have shown that Daam2 potentiates canonical Wnt signaling through the clustering of existing Wnt receptor complexes (Lee and Deneen, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee and Deneen, 2012.

claim: Mutations in key components of the Wnt-pathway and dysregulated Wnt-signaling has not been widely linked to low- or high-grade glioma.
source: While the Wnt pathway has been implicated in several forms of cancer, including medulloblastoma, mutations in key components of the Wnt-pathway and dysregulated Wnt-signaling has not been widely linked to low- or high-grade glioma (Bienz and Clevers, 2000; de La Coste et al., 1998; Klaus and Birchmeier, 2008; Lustig and Behrens, 2003; Morin et al., 1997; Rubinfeld et al., 1997; Zurawel et al., 1998).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Daam1 and Daam2 have highly conserved formin domains yet exhibit non-overlapping expression patterns in the developing CNS.
source: Daam1 and Daam2 have highly conserved formin domains yet exhibit non-overlapping expression patterns in the developing CNS (Habas et al., 2001; Kida et al., 2004; Lee and Deneen, 2012; Nakaya et al., 2004), suggesting distinct functions during development.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Daam2 functions via canonical Wnt-signaling during CNS development.
source: Indeed, Daam2 functions in this context via canonical Wnt-signaling, while Daam1 operates via the non-canonical Wnt, planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway (Habas et al., 2001; Lee and Deneen, 2012; Li et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Daam1 operates via the non-canonical Wnt, planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway during CNS development.
source: Indeed, Daam2 functions in this context via canonical Wnt-signaling, while Daam1 operates via the non-canonical Wnt, planar cell polarity (PCP) pathway (Habas et al., 2001; Lee and Deneen, 2012; Li et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2008; Zhu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The PCP pathway has been implicated in tumor cell invasion and migration.
source: Given that the PCP pathway has been implicated in tumor cell invasion and migration (Anastas and Moon, 2013; Paw et al., 2015; Weeraratna et al., 2002), it is possible that Daam-family proteins also contribute to these features of tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Daam1, Daam2 and other formin-family genes have been implicated in the migration of breast and neuroblastoma cell lines.
source: Recent studies have implicated Daam1, Daam2 and other formin-family genes in the migration of breast and neuroblastoma cell lines (Luga et al., 2012), respectively, suggesting that the Daam-family proteins may also contribute to invasion and metastasis in other malignancies.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Luga et al., 2012.

claim: Daam2 is expressed in both glial lineages (oligodendrocytes and astrocytes), in both precursor and mature stages of development.
source: Daam2 is expressed in both glial lineages (oligodendrocytes and astrocytes), in both precursor and mature stages of development.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Daam2 functions to suppress the differentiation of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPC) during development and after injury.
source: Another feature of Daam2 is that it functions to suppress the differentiation of oligodendrocyte progenitor cells (OPC) during development and after injury (Lee et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2015.

claim: OPCs may serve as a cell of origin for glioma.
source: Studies in mouse models suggest that OPCs may serve as a cell of origin for glioma, while NG2-positive OPC populations are endowed with tumor initiating properties (Ligon et al., 2007; Liu et al., 2011; Persson et al., 2010; Stiles and Rowitch, 2008; Sugiarto et al., 2011; Yadavilli et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The VHL-HIF1α signaling axis has been linked to OPC development and neonatal hypoxic injury responses.
source: Indeed recent studies have linked the VHL-HIF1α signaling axis to OPC development and neonatal hypoxic injury responses (Yuen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Yuen et al., 2014.

claim: Inactivating mutations in VHL are predominately found in ccRCC and are very rare in most other forms of cancer, including glioma.
source: Importantly, inactivating mutations in VHL are predominately found in ccRCC and are very rare in most other forms of cancer, including glioma.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHL mutations in cancer.

claim: VHL can be degraded via the Hsp70 and Hsp110 chaperone system in yeast.
source: Interestingly, prior studies in yeast have shown that VHL can be degraded via the Hsp70 and Hsp110 chaperone system (McClellan et al., 2005; Melville et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to McClellan et al., 2005 and Melville et al., 2003.

claim: Hsp's are expressed across a host of cancers.
source: Given that Hsp's are expressed across a host of cancers (García-Morales et al., 2007; Nylandsted et al., 2002; Sauvageot et al., 2009), it will be important to determine whether Daam2 engages the Hsp chaperone system to facilitate VHL degradation in glioma and other malignancies.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: ID2 interference with VHL activity can deregulate HIF1α expression and promote tumorigenesis in xenograft models.
source: Studies in glioma cell lines suggest that ID2 interference with VHL activity can deregulate HIF1α expression and promote tumorigenesis in xenograft models (Lee et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2016.

claim: ID2 has been linked to the suppression of OPC differentiation via direct regulation of cell cycle kinetics.
source: Interestingly, ID2 has also been linked to the suppression of OPC differentiation via direct regulation of cell cycle kinetics (Wang et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wang et al., 2001.

claim: Both ID2 and Daam2 suppress VHL, inhibit OPC differentiation, and promote glioma tumorigenesis.
source: These observations further reinforce the relationship between OPC development and glioma tumorigenesis and highlight key parallels between ID2 and Daam2 function across these systems, as both genes suppress VHL, inhibit OPC differentiation, and promote glioma tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is based on inference from the data presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: VHL functions as an E3 ligase.
source: Given that VHL functions as an E3 ligase and associates with Daam2, this may be another mechanism by which this complex operates.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VHL function.

claim: Dysregulation of ubiquitination is linked to protein aggregation associated with several neurological disorders.
source: Indeed dysregulation of ubiquitination is linked to protein aggregation associated with several neurological disorders, functioning through both neuronal and glial populations (Jansen et al., 2014 and Hegde and Upadhya, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Jansen et al., 2014 and Hegde and Upadhya, 2007.

claim: OPCs have latent proliferative capacity that is essential for injury responses.
source: Moreover, OPCs have latent proliferative capacity that is essential for injury responses, suggesting parallels between the processes that drive injury responses and tumorigenesis.
evidence: This is established knowledge about OPC biology.

claim: Daam2 overexpression in GBM1 cell line results in approximately 3-fold increase in cell number by day 9 compared to control.
source: Figure 2A
evidence: This can be inferred from the cell proliferation graph in Figure 2A showing GBM-1 cell line growth over 9 days.

claim: Daam2 overexpression results in approximately 1.5-fold increase in soft agar colony formation in GBM1 cell line.
source: Each of these in vitro experiments was performed in triplicate and replicated three times; quantification is in E, **p=0.036.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2E with statistical significance.

claim: Daam2 overexpression in CRISPR-IUE glioma results in approximately 6-fold increase in luciferase activity at 7 weeks compared to control.
source: Imaging quantification in I is derived from 7 Daam2-overexpression and eight control mice; *p=0.0079.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2I with statistical significance.

claim: Daam2 overexpression in CRISPR-IUE glioma results in approximately 2-fold increase in BrdU-positive cells compared to control.
source: Relative number of BrdU expressing cells is quantified in L and is derived from six total mice, four slides per mouse, from each experimental condition; ***p=0.0019.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 2L with statistical significance.

claim: Daam2-shRNAi reduces Daam2 mRNA expression to approximately 10% of scrambled control levels in GBM1 cell line.
source: Figure 3A
evidence: This can be inferred from the qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Daam2-shRNAi in GBM1 cell line reduces tumor growth to approximately 30% of scrambled control at 6 weeks post-transplantation.
source: Imaging quantification is derived from seven mice transplanted with GBM1/Daam2-shRNAi and 5 GBM1/scrambled controls; *p=0.0325.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 3E with statistical significance.

claim: Daam2 knockout in CRISPR-IUE glioma results in approximately 30% of the luciferase activity compared to Daam2+/- controls at 8 weeks.
source: Imaging quantification is derived from 8 Daam2-/- and 9 Daam2 ± mice; **p=0.0049.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 3H with statistical significance.

claim: Daam2 knockout in CRISPR-IUE glioma results in approximately 50% reduction in BrdU-positive cells compared to Daam2+/- controls.
source: Relative number of BrdU expressing cells is quantified in K and is derived from six total mice, four slides per mouse, from each experimental condition; ****p=0.00001.
evidence: This is shown in the quantification in Figure 3K with statistical significance.

claim: Overexpression of mouse Daam2 rescues the growth defects in Daam2-shRNAi knockdown cell lines.
source: Rescue of growth defects manifest in Daam2-shRNAi knockdown cell lines via overexpression of mouse Daam2. In both cases overexpression of mouse Daam2 in the presence of the Daam2-shRNAi (blue line) rescued the growth defects present with Daam2-shRNAi alone (red line).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Daam2 and VHL demonstrate an inverse correlation with r=-0.19 and p<1E-25 across multiple cancer types in TCGA data.
source: This analysis identified von Hippel Landau (VHL) as one of the proteins from this cohort with the most significant inverse correlation score across this spectrum of malignancies, with lung adenocarcinoma and GBM demonstrating the strongest negative correlations between Daam2 and VHL (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Daam2 and HIF1α demonstrate a positive correlation with r=0.09 and p<1E-6 across multiple cancer types in TCGA data.
source: Analysis of these data revealed that Daam2 expression was positively correlated with HIF1α and pAkt protein expression across this cohort of malignancies, with GBM and lung adenocarcinoma also showing the strongest positive correlation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 4B.

claim: Daam2 and AKT pS473 demonstrate a positive correlation with r=0.27 and p<1E-50 across multiple cancer types in TCGA data.
source: Analysis of these data revealed that Daam2 expression was positively correlated with HIF1α and pAkt protein expression across this cohort of malignancies, with GBM and lung adenocarcinoma also showing the strongest positive correlation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in the correlation analysis in Figure 4B.
